references.text: The immediate context: [ref:Joh 5:2-3|John 5:2-3] describes the Pool of Bethesda and the sick who lay there waiting for the water to be stirred – the situation that verse 4 explains the background for.

In [ref:Joh 5:7|John 5:7], the sick man says he has no one to help him into the pool when the water is stirred, which presupposes the belief described in verse 4 that the first person to step into the water after it was stirred would be healed.

In [ref:Joh 9:6-7|John 9:6-7], Jesus sends the blind man to the Pool of Siloam to wash and be healed – another event where water and healing are connected, but where the power comes from Jesus himself.
In [ref:2 Kong 5:10-14|2 Kings 5:10-14], Naaman is healed of leprosy by dipping himself in the Jordan River. This parallels the motif in John 5:4, where healing occurs through stepping into water.

[ref:Esek 47:8-9|Ezekiel 47:8-9] describes healing water flowing out from the temple and bringing life. This is a prophetic vision of supernatural healing water, forming the background for the motif of healing water in the Pool of Bethesda.

[ref:Hebr 1:14|Hebrews 1:14] describes angels as ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation. John 5:4 describes an angel sent with a healing mission – a concrete example of such angelic service.

[ref:Sal 103:3|Psalm 103:3] praises the Lord as the one who heals all diseases. Verse 4 describes healing from every disease (ᾧ δήποτε κατείχετο νοσήματι), and it is God who is the source of this healing through his angel.

[ref:Sal 104:4|Psalm 104:4] says that God makes his angels winds and his servants flames of fire. This emphasizes that angels carry out God's will as his messengers, just as the angel in John 5:4 carries out a healing mission at the Pool of Bethesda.
